uncing%20ball%2C%20a%20pendulum%2C%20a%20person%20walking%2C%20a%20mass%20on%20a%20spring%2C%20or%20something%20else.%20What%20variable%20would%20you%20measure%20to%20describe%20its%20state%3F%0A%20%20%20%20%22%22%22)%0A%20%20%20%20return%0A%0A%0A%40app.cell(hide_code%3DTrue)%0Adef%20_(mo)%3A%0A%20%20%20%20mo.md(r%22%22%22%0A%20%20%20%20%23%23%20Python%20setup%0A%0A%20%20%20%20NumPy%20stores%20the%20numerical%20states%2C%20Matplotlib%20draws%20the%20trajectories%2C%20and%20SciPy%20provides%20%60solve_ivp%60.%20All%20inputs%20are%20stated%20model%20parameters%3B%20no%20external%20dataset%20is%20needed.%20Run%20the%20examples%20and%20compare%20step%20sizes%20before%20trusting%20a%20trajectory.%20Expand%20exercise%20solutions%20only%20after%20trying%20the%20update%20yourself.%0A%20%20%20%20%22%22%22)%0A%20%20%20%20return%0A%0A%0A%40app.cell(hide_code%3DTrue)%0Adef%20_(mo)%3A%0A%20%20%20%20mo.md(r%22%22%22%0A%20%20%20%20%23%23%20An%20unassuming%20derivation%20of%20a%20numerical%20solution%20to%20an%20Ordinary%20Differential%20Equation%20(ODE)%0A%0A%20%20%20%20Imagine%20you%20are%20in%20a%20car.%20You%20want%20to%20know%20where%20the%20car%20is%20at%20each%20moment%2C%20but%20you%20do%20not%20have%20a%20formula%20for%20its%20position.%20What%20you%20do%20have%20is%20simpler%3A%20the%20initial%20position%20of%20the%20car%20and%20measurements%20of%20its%20speed%20from%20time%20to%20time.%0A%0A%20%20%20%20That%20is%20already%20enough%20to%20make%20progress.%0A%0A%20%20%20%20Velocity%20tells%20us%20how%20fast%20position%20is%20changing%3A%0A%0A%20%20%20%20%24%24%0A%20%20%20%20v(t)%20%3D%20%5Cfrac%7B%5Cmathrm%7Bd%7Dx(t)%7D%7B%5Cmathrm%7Bd%7Dt%7D.%0A%20%20%20%20%24%24%0A%0A%20%20%20%20The%20notation%20%5C(x(t)%5C)%20and%20%5C(v(t)%5C)%20is%20just%20a%20reminder%20that%20both%20position%20and%20velocity%20can%20change%20with%20time.%0A%0A%20%20%20%20If%20we%20look%20at%20two%20nearby%20instants%2C%20we%20can%20approximate%20the%20velocity%20by%20asking%20how%20much%20the%20position%20changed%20during%20that%20time%20interval%3A%0A%0A%20%20%20%20%24%24%0A%20%20%20%20v_i%20%5Capprox%20%5Cfrac%7Bx_%7Bi%2B1%7D%20-%20x_i%7D%7Bt_%7Bi%2B1%7D%20-%20t_i%7D.%0A%20%20%20%20%24%24%0A%0A%20%20%20%20Here%2C%20%5C(i%5C)%20labels%20one%20measured%20instant%20and%20%5C(i%2B1%5C)%20labels%20the%20next%20one.%20To%20keep%20the%20first%20idea%20simple%2C%20suppose%20the%20measurements%20are%20equally%20spaced%20in%20time.%20Then%0A%0A%20%20%20%20%24%24%0A%20%20%20%20t_%7Bi%2B1%7D%20-%20t_i%20%3D%20%5CDelta%20t%2C%0A%20%20%20%20%24%24%0A%0A%20%20%20%20and%20the%20approximation%20becomes%0A%0A%20%20%20%20%24%24%0A%20%20%20%20v_i%20%5Capprox%20%5Cfrac%7Bx_%7Bi%2B1%7D%20-%20x_i%7D%7B%5CDelta%20t%7D.%0A%20%20%20%20%24%24%0A%0A%20%20%20%20Now%20comes%20the%20useful%20trick.%20Rearrange%20this%20expression%20to%20isolate%20the%20next%20position%3A%0A%0A%20%20%20%20%24%24%0A%20%20%20%20x_%7Bi%2B1%7D%20%5Capprox%20x_i%20%2B%20v_i%20%5CDelta%20t.%0A%20%20%20%20%24%24%0A%0A%20%20%20%20This%20says%20something%20very%20practical%3A%20if%20you%20know%20where%20the%20car%20is%20now%2C%20and%20you%20know%20its%20current%20speed%2C%20you%20can%20estimate%20where%20it%20will%20be%20after%20one%20small%20time%20step.%0A%0A%20%20%20%20For%20example%2C%20suppose%0A%0A%20%20%20%20%24%24%0A%20%20%20%20x_0%20%3D%20100%5C%20%5Cmathrm%7Bm%7D%2C%20%5Cqquad%20v_0%20%3D%2020%5C%20%5Cmathrm%7Bm%2Fs%7D%2C%20%5Cqquad%20%5CDelta%20t%20%3D%2010%5C%20%5Cmathrm%7Bs%7D.%0A%20%20%20%20%24%24%0A%0A%20%20%20%20Then%0A%0A%20%20%20%20%24%24%0A%20%20%20%20x_1%20%5Capprox%20100%20%2B%2020%20%5Ccdot%2010%20%3D%20300%5C%20%5Cmathrm%7Bm%7D.%0A%20%20%20%20%24%24%0A%0A%20%20%20%20The%20index%20%5C(1%5C)%20means%20the%20next%20measured%20instant%2C%20which%20in%20this%20example%20is%20%5C(t%3D10%5C)%20s.%0A%0A%20%20%20%20Now%20suppose%20that%20at%20%5C(t%3D10%5C)%20s%20the%20measured%20speed%20is%0A%0A%20%20%20%20%24%24%0A%20%20%20%20v_1%20%3D%2025%5C%20%5Cmathrm%7Bm%2Fs%7D.%0A%20%20%20%20%24%24%0A%0A%20%20%20%20Because%20we%20already%20estimated%20%5C(x_1%5C)%2C%20we%20can%20repeat%20the%20same%20step%3A%0A%0A%20%20%20%20%24%24%0A%20%20%20%20x_2%20%5Capprox%20x_1%20%2B%20v_1%20%5CDelta%20t%2C%0A%20%20%20%20%24%24%0A%0A%20%20%20%20so%0A%0A%20%20%20%20%24%24%0A%20%20%20%20x_2%20%5Capprox%20300%20%2B%2025%20%5Ccdot%2010%20%3D%20550%5C%20%5Cmathrm%7Bm%7D.%0A%20%20%20%20%24%24%0A%0A%20%20%20%20Another%20way%20to%20see%20the%20same%20calculation%20is%20to%20keep%20a%20running%20table.%20The%20position%20in%20each%20row%20is%20the%20position%20after%20applying%20the%20speed%20from%20the%20previous%20interval%3A%0A%0A%20%20%20%20%7C%20%5C(i%5C)%20%7C%20Time%20%5C(t_i%5C)%20%5Bs%5D%20%7C%20Speed%20used%20over%20previous%20interval%20%5Bm%2Fs%5D%20%7C%20Position%20%5C(x_i%5C)%20%5Bm%5D%20%7C%0A%20%20%20%20%7C---%3A%7C---%3A%7C---%3A%7C---%3A%7C%0A%20%20%20%20%7C%200%20%7C%200%20%7C%20--%20%7C%20100%20%7C%0A%20%20%20%20%7C%201%20%7C%2010%20%7C%2020%20%7C%20300%20%7C%0A%20%20%20%20%7C%202%20%7C%2020%20%7C%2025%20%7C%20550%20%7C%0A%20%20%20%20%7C%203%20%7C%2030%20%7C%2030%20%7C%20%3F%20%7C%0A%0A%20%20%20%20The%20first%20row%20is%20the%20initial%20condition.%20The%20second%20row%20uses%20%5C(v_0%3D20%5C%20%5Cmathrm%7Bm%2Fs%7D%5C)%2C%20and%20the%20third%20row%20uses%20%5C(v_1%3D25%5C%20%5Cmathrm%7Bm%2Fs%7D%5C).%20Calculate%20the%20new%20position%20at%20%5C(t%3D30%5C%20%5Cmathrm%7Bs%7D%5C).%0A%0A%20%20%20%20And%20there%20is%20the%20pattern%3A%0A%0A%20%20%20%20%24%24%0A%20%20%20%20x_%7Bi%2B1%7D%20%5Capprox%20x_i%20%2B%20v_i%20%5CDelta%20t.%0A%20%20%20%20%24%24%0A%0A%20%20%20%20To%20estimate%20the%20position%20farther%20into%20the%20future%2C%20we%20do%20not%20jump%20there%20all%20at%20once.%20We%20move%20step%20by%20step%2C%20always%20using%20the%20current%20position%20and%20the%20current%20velocity%20to%20estimate%20the%20next%20position.%0A%0A%20%20%20%20This%20is%20the%20basic%20idea%20behind%20Euler's%20method%20for%20numerically%20solving%20a%20first-order%20ordinary%20differential%20equation%3A%0A%0A%20%20%20%20%24%24%0A%20%20%20%20%5Cfrac%7B%5Cmathrm%7Bd%7Dx(t)%7D%7B%5Cmathrm%7Bd%7Dt%7D%20%3D%20v(t).%0A%20%20%20%20%24%24%0A%0A%20%20%20%20In%20this%20example%3A%0A%0A%20%20%20%20-%20%5C(x_0%5C)%20is%20the%20initial%20condition%3B%0A%20%20%20%20-%20%5C(v(t)%5C)%20gives%20the%20rate%20of%20change%20of%20position%3B%0A%20%20%20%20-%20%5C(%5CDelta%20t%5C)%20is%20the%20time%20step%3B%0A%20%20%20%20-%20%5C(x_%7Bi%2B1%7D%20%5Capprox%20x_i%20%2B%20v_i%5CDelta%20t%5C)%20is%20the%20Euler%20update.%0A%0A%20%20%20%20Notice%20what%20we%20obtained%3A%20a%20list%20of%20estimated%20positions%20at%20selected%20times.%20We%20did%20not%20obtain%20a%20single%20formula%20for%20%5C(x(t)%5C).%20That%20is%20what%20makes%20this%20a%20numerical%20solution.%20Because%20we%20started%20with%20speed%20and%20estimated%20position%20by%20summing%20increments%2C%20this%20process%20is%20numerical%20integration.%0A%20%20%20%20Because%20the%20calculation%20starts%20from%20a%20known%20initial%20value%2C%20this%20kind%20of%20problem%20is%20called%20an%20initial%20value%20problem%2C%20or%20IVP.%0A%0A%20%20%20%20**The%20case%20when%20only%20the%20acceleration%20is%20known**%0A%20%20%20%20Now%20imagine%20that%20we%20only%20have%20access%20to%20the%20car's%20acceleration%2C%20for%20example%20from%20a%20smartphone%20accelerometer%2C%20and%20that%20we%20know%20the%20initial%20position%20and%20speed.%20Can%20we%20still%20find%20the%20position%20at%20a%20later%20time%3F%20Let's%20try%20a%20similar%20approach%20for%20this%20more%20challenging%20problem.%0A%0A%20%20%20%20Acceleration%20tells%20us%20how%20fast%20velocity%20is%20changing%3A%0A%0A%20%20%20%20%24%24%0A%20%20%20%20a(t)%20%3D%20%5Cfrac%7B%5Cmathrm%7Bd%7Dv(t)%7D%7B%5Cmathrm%7Bd%7Dt%7D.%0A%20%20%20%20%24%24%0A%0A%20%20%20%20If%20the%20acceleration%20is%20measured%20at%20equally%20spaced%20instants%2C%20we%20can%20use%20the%20same%20finite-difference%20idea%3A%0A%0A%20%20%20%20%24%24%0A%20%20%20%20a_i%20%5Capprox%20%5Cfrac%7Bv_%7Bi%2B1%7D%20-%20v_i%7D%7B%5CDelta%20t%7D.%0A%20%20%20%20%24%24%0A%0A%20%20%20%20Rearranging%20gives%20an%20update%20for%20the%20next%20speed%3A%0A%0A%20%20%20%20%24%24%0A%20%20%20%20v_%7Bi%2B1%7D%20%5Capprox%20v_i%20%2B%20a_i%5CDelta%20t.%0A%20%20%20%20%24%24%0A%0A%20%20%20%20Alongside%20that%2C%20we%20keep%20using%20the%20current%20speed%20to%20update%20position.%20So%20the%20state%20we%20carry%20from%20one%20row%20to%20the%20next%20is%20not%20just%20position%20anymore%3B%20it%20is%20the%20pair%20%5C((x_i%2C%20v_i)%5C).%20In%20the%20simplest%20Euler%20version%2C%20the%20next%20state%20is%20defined%20by%20these%20two%20coupled%20equations%3A%0A%0A%20%20%20%20%24%24%0A%20%20%20%20%5Cleft%5C%7B%0A%20%20%20%20%5Cbegin%7Barray%7D%7Bl%7D%0A%20%20%20%20x_%7Bi%2B1%7D%20%5Capprox%20x_i%20%2B%20v_i%5CDelta%20t%2C%5C%5C%0A%20%20%20%20v_%7Bi%2B1%7D%20%5Capprox%20v_i%20%2B%20a_i%5CDelta%20t.%0A%20%20%20%20%5Cend%7Barray%7D%0A%20%20%20%20%5Cright.%0A%20%20%20%20%24%24%0A%0A%20%20%20%20They%20are%20coupled%20because%20the%20position%20update%20needs%20the%20current%20speed%2C%20and%20the%20speed%20update%20needs%20the%20current%20acceleration.%20This%20idea%20will%20come%20back%20later%20when%20we%20rewrite%20higher-order%20ODEs%20as%20systems%20of%20first-order%20equations.%0A%0A%20%20%20%20Suppose%20the%20car%20starts%20at%20%5C(x_0%3D100%5C%20%5Cmathrm%7Bm%7D%5C)%2C%20starts%20with%20%5C(v_0%3D20%5C%20%5Cmathrm%7Bm%2Fs%7D%5C)%2C%20and%20%5C(%5CDelta%20t%3D10%5C%20%5Cmathrm%7Bs%7D%5C).%20If%20the%20first%20three%20acceleration%20measurements%20are%20%5C(a_0%3D0.5%5C%20%5Cmathrm%7Bm%2Fs%5E2%7D%5C)%2C%20%5C(a_1%3D0.5%5C%20%5Cmathrm%7Bm%2Fs%5E2%7D%5C)%2C%20and%20%5C(a_2%3D0.5%5C%20%5Cmathrm%7Bm%2Fs%5E2%7D%5C)%2C%20the%20calculation%20looks%20like%20this%3A%0A%0A%20%20%20%20%7C%20%5C(i%5C)%20%7C%20Time%20%5C(t_i%5C)%20%5Bs%5D%20%7C%20Acceleration%20used%20over%20next%20interval%20%5Bm%2Fs%5E2%5D%20%7C%20Speed%20%5C(v_i%5C)%20%5Bm%2Fs%5D%20%7C%20Position%20%5C(x_i%5C)%20%5Bm%5D%20%7C%0A%20%20%20%20%7C---%3A%7C---%3A%7C---%3A%7C---%3A%7C---%3A%7C%0A%20%20%20%20%7C%200%20%7C%200%20%7C%200.5%20%7C%2020%20%7C%20100%20%7C%0A%20%20%20%20%7C%201%20%7C%2010%20%7C%200.5%20%7C%2025%20%7C%20300%20%7C%0A%20%20%20%20%7C%202%20%7C%2020%20%7C%200.5%20%7C%2030%20%7C%20550%20%7C%0A%20%20%20%20%7C%203%20%7C%2030%20%7C%20--%20%7C%2035%20%7C%20%3F%20%7C%0A%0A%20%20%20%20Use%20the%20row%20at%20%5C(t%3D20%5C%20%5Cmathrm%7Bs%7D%5C)%20to%20calculate%20the%20new%20position%20at%20%5C(t%3D30%5C%20%5Cmathrm%7Bs%7D%5C).%20Here%2C%20acceleration%20is%20first%20accumulated%20into%20speed%2C%20and%20speed%20is%20then%20accumulated%20into%20position.%20This%20is%20a%20double%20numerical%20integration%3A%20acceleration%20to%20velocity%2C%20then%20velocity%20to%20position.%0A%0A%20%20%20%20Next%20we%20will%20switch%20to%20a%20more%20formal%20description%20of%20ordinary%20differential%20equations%20and%20work%20through%20more%20examples.%20If%20a%20problem%20starts%20to%20feel%20abstract%2C%20come%20back%20to%20the%20car%3A%20ask%20which%20quantities%20play%20the%20role%20of%20position%20and%20velocity%2C%20and%20which%20equation%20is%20giving%20you%20the%20acceleration-like%20rate%20of%20change.%20Once%20those%20pieces%20are%20named%2C%20the%20numerical%20task%20is%20the%20same%20kind%20of%20step-by-step%20update.%0A%0A%20%20%20%20**Challenge%201.**%20Write%20a%20pseudocode%20to%20implement%20the%20Euler's%20method%20for%20numerically%20solving%20a%20first-order%20ordinary%20differential%20equation.%0A%20%20%20%20%22%22%22)%0A%20%20%20%20return%0A%0A%0A%40app.cell(hide_code%3DTrue)%0Adef%20_(mo)%3A%0A%20%20%20%20mo.md(r%22%22%22%0A%20%20%20%20**Exercise%201.**%20Complete%20the%20car%20table%20at%2030%20s.%20What%20would%20the%20exact%20position%20be%20under%20constant%20acceleration%200.5%20m%2Fs%C2%B2%3F%0A%0A%20%20%20%20%2F%2F%2F%20details%20%7C%20Solution%20to%20Exercise%201%0A%20%20%20%20Forward%20Euler%20gives%20%24550%2B30(10)%3D850%24%20m.%20The%20exact%20constant-acceleration%20result%20is%20%24100%2B20(30)%2B0.5(0.5)(30)%5E2%3D925%24%20m.%20The%20method%20used%20the%20speed%20at%20the%20start%20of%20each%20interval%20and%20therefore%20underestimated%20the%20distance%20during%20acceleration.%0A%20%20%20%20%2F%2F%2F%0A%20%20%20%20%22%22%22)%0A%20%20%20%20return%0A%0A%0A%40app.cell(hide_code%3DTrue)%0Adef%20_(mo)%3A%0A%20%20%20%20mo.md(r%22%22%22%0A%20%20%20%20%23%23%20Ordinary%20Differential%20Equation%0A%0A%20%20%20%20An%20ODE%20is%20an%20equation%20that%20relates%20a%20function%20of%20one%20independent%20variable%20to%20one%20or%20more%20of%20its%20derivatives.%20In%20this%20tutorial%2C%20the%20independent%20variable%20will%20usually%20be%20time.%20Solving%20an%20ODE%20means%20finding%20a%20function%20whose%20derivatives%20satisfy%20that%20relationship.%0A%0A%20%20%20%20The%20order%20of%20an%20ODE%20is%20the%20order%20of%20its%20highest%20derivative.%20For%20example%2C%20a%20first-order%20ODE%20contains%20only%20first%20derivatives.%20A%20linear%20ODE%20is%20linear%20in%20the%20unknown%20function%20and%20its%20derivatives%3B%20many%20important%20linear%20ODEs%20have%20analytical%20solutions%2C%20but%20others%20are%20still%20solved%20numerically%20in%20practice.%20Nonlinear%20ODEs%20can%20sometimes%20be%20solved%20exactly%2C%20but%20numerical%20methods%20are%20often%20the%20practical%20approach.%0A%0A%20%20%20%20A%20partial%20differential%20equation%20contains%20partial%20derivatives%20of%20an%20unknown%20function%20of%20several%20independent%20variables%2C%20such%20as%20both%20position%20and%20time.%0A%0A%20%20%20%20Newton's%20second%20law%20gives%20a%20simple%20example%3A%0A%0A%20%20%20%20%24%24%0A%20%20%20%20m%5Cfrac%7B%5Cmathrm%7Bd%7D%5E2%20%5Cmathbf%7Bx%7D%7D%7B%5Cmathrm%7Bd%7Dt%5E2%7D(t)%20%3D%20%5Cmathbf%7BF%7D.%0A%20%20%20%20%24%24%0A%0A%20%20%20%20Here%2C%20%24%5Cmathbf%7Bx%7D(t)%24%20is%20the%20position%20as%20a%20function%20of%20time%20and%20%24t%24%20is%20the%20independent%20variable.%20The%20force%20%24%5Cmathbf%7BF% 20%20**Exercise%207.**%20Classify%20the%20damping%20cases%20%24c%3D0%24%2C%201.2%2C%20and%2010%20for%20%24m%3D1%24%2C%20%24k%3D25%24.%20Does%20arbitrarily%20large%20damping%20always%20return%20the%20system%20faster%3F%0A%0A%20%20%20%20%2F%2F%2F%20details%20%7C%20Solution%20to%20Exercise%207%0A%20%20%20%20The%20critical%20coefficient%20is%20%242%5Csqrt%7Bmk%7D%3D10%24.%20The%20cases%20are%20undamped%2C%20underdamped%2C%20and%20critically%20damped.%20Very%20large%20damping%20produces%20a%20slow%20overdamped%20response%2C%20so%20%E2%80%9Cmore%20damping%E2%80%9D%20is%20not%20synonymous%20with%20%E2%80%9Cfaster%20return%E2%80%9D.%0A%20%20%20%20%2F%2F%2F%0A%20%20%20%20%22%22%22)%0A%20%20%20%20return%0A%0A%0A%40app.cell(hide_code%3DTrue)%0Adef%20_(mo)%3A%0A%20%20%20%20mo.md(r%22%22%22%0A%20%20%20%20%23%23%20Checkpoint%20questions%0A%0A%20%20%20%20Pause%20here%20before%20the%20final%20problems.%20These%20questions%20connect%20the%20examples%20in%20this%20notebook%20with%20mechanics%20examples%20used%20elsewhere%20in%20the%20course.%0A%0A%20%20%20%201.%20In%20the%20football-with-drag%20example%2C%20what%20would%20terminal%20velocity%20mean%3F%20Which%20term%20in%20the%20ODE%20prevents%20the%20downward%20speed%20from%20growing%20without%20bound%3F%0A%20%20%20%202.%20In%20a%20one-mass%20spring%20problem%2C%20why%20is%20the%20displacement%20usually%20measured%20from%20the%20equilibrium%20position%20instead%20of%20from%20the%20unstretched%20spring%20length%3F%0A%20%20%20%203.%20If%20you%20had%20a%20force-platform%20record%20from%20a%20vertical%20jump%2C%20which%20signal%20would%20you%20integrate%20to%20estimate%20velocity%3F%20What%20initial%20condition%20would%20you%20need%3F%0A%20%20%20%204.%20A%20two-mass%20spring-damper%20system%20needs%20more%20state%20variables%20than%20the%20one-mass%20example.%20What%20are%20the%20minimum%20state%20variables%20if%20the%20two%20masses%20move%20only%20along%20one%20horizontal%20line%3F%0A%20%20%20%205.%20In%20a%20simple%20muscle-tendon%20model%2C%20which%20elements%20would%20behave%20like%20springs%2C%20which%20element%20would%20behave%20like%20a%20damper%2C%20and%20which%20element%20would%20represent%20active%20force%20production%3F%0A%20%20%20%206.%20When%20would%20you%20trust%20a%20coarse%20Euler%20solution%20for%20teaching%20or%20estimation%2C%20and%20when%20would%20you%20switch%20to%20%60solve_ivp%60%20with%20tighter%20tolerances%3F%0A%20%20%20%20%22%22%22)%0A%20%20%20%20return%0A%0A%0A%40app.cell(hide_code%3DTrue)%0Adef%20_(mo)%3A%0A%20%20%20%20mo.md(r%22%22%22%0A%20%20%20%20%2F%2F%2F%20details%20%7C%20Checkpoint%20answers%0A%20%20%20%201.%20Terminal%20velocity%20is%20a%20downward%20steady%20speed%20where%20drag%20balances%20weight%3B%20the%20quadratic%20term%20limits%20acceleration.%0A%20%20%20%202.%20The%20static%20preload%20can%20then%20be%20absorbed%20into%20the%20equilibrium%20definition.%0A%20%20%20%203.%20Integrate%20%24(F_z-mg)%2Fm%24%2C%20starting%20from%20a%20known%20center-of-mass%20velocity.%0A%20%20%20%204.%20Two%20positions%20and%20two%20velocities.%0A%20%20%20%205.%20Tendon%20and%20passive%20elastic%20tissue%20are%20spring-like%3B%20viscous%20tissue%20is%20damper-like%3B%20the%20contractile%20element%20supplies%20active%20force.%0A%20%20%20%206.%20Use%20step%20refinement%20and%20comparison%20with%20a%20known%20solution%20or%20tighter%20reference.%20Switch%20when%20numerical%20error%20matters%20for%20the%20question%3B%20choose%20tolerances%20against%20a%20physical%20accuracy%20requirement.%0A%20%20%20%20%2F%2F%2F%0A%20%20%20%20%22%22%22)%0A%20%20%20%20return%0A%0A%0A%40app.cell(hide_code%3DTrue)%0Adef%20_(mo)%3A%0A%20%20%20%20mo.md(r%22%22%22%0A%20%20%20%20%23%23%20Problems%0A%0A%20%20%20%20Work%20through%20these%20in%20order%20if%20you%20are%20studying%20independently.%20For%20each%20one%2C%20first%20write%20the%20IVP%20on%20paper%2C%20then%20modify%20or%20reuse%20code%20from%20this%20notebook.%0A%0A%20%20%20%201.%20**IVP%20audit.**%20Explain%20in%20your%20own%20words%20why%20an%20IVP%20needs%20both%20a%20differential%20equation%20and%20an%20initial%20condition.%20Then%20give%20one%20example%20where%20changing%20only%20the%20initial%20condition%20changes%20the%20entire%20motion.%0A%0A%20%20%20%202.%20**Pendulum%20amplitude.**%20For%20the%20pendulum%2C%20change%20only%20the%20initial%20angular%20velocity.%20What%20changes%20in%20the%20plot%20and%20what%20stays%20similar%3F%20Repeat%20with%20initial%20angles%20of%20%2410%5E%5Ccirc%24%2C%20%2445%5E%5Ccirc%24%2C%20and%20%2490%5E%5Ccirc%24.%0A%0A%20%20%20%203.%20**Projectile%20with%20terminal%20velocity.**%20A%20%2410%24%20kg%20projectile%20is%20launched%20vertically%20upward%20with%20%24v_0%3D50%5C%2C%5Cmathrm%7Bm%2Fs%7D%24.%20Compare%20the%20maximum%20height%20when%20drag%20is%20neglected%20with%20the%20height%20when%20the%20drag%20force%20is%20%24F_D%3D0.01v%7Cv%7C%24.%20Does%20the%20object%20approach%20a%20terminal%20velocity%20on%20the%20way%20down%3F%0A%0A%20%20%20%204.%20**Euler%20step-size%20audit.**%20For%20the%20football%20example%2C%20find%20a%20step%20size%20for%20Euler's%20method%20that%20makes%20the%20position%20error%20visually%20small.%20How%20small%20is%20small%20enough%20for%20your%20purpose%3F%20Explain%20your%20criterion.%0A%0A%20%20%20%205.%20**Two-dimensional%20projectile%20IVP.**%20Extend%20the%20vertical%20football%20model%20to%20two%20dimensions.%20Use%20state%20variables%20%24x%24%2C%20%24y%24%2C%20%24v_x%24%2C%20and%20%24v_y%24.%20Then%20add%20drag%20forces%20that%20oppose%20each%20velocity%20component.%0A%0A%20%20%20%206.%20**Design%20a%20mass-spring-damper%20system.**%20Use%20mass%20%24m%3D2%24%20kg%20and%20choose%20stiffness%20and%20damping%20values%20so%20the%20system%20returns%20close%20to%20equilibrium%20quickly%20but%20does%20not%20oscillate%20more%20than%20once.%20Report%20the%20values%20you%20tried%20and%20justify%20your%20final%20choice.%0A%0A%20%20%20%207.%20**One-mass%20spring%20problem.**%20A%20%241%24%20kg%20block%20is%20attached%20to%20a%20spring%20with%20stiffness%20%24k%3D100%5C%2C%5Cmathrm%7BN%2Fm%7D%24.%20At%20%24t%3D0%24%2C%20the%20block%20is%20displaced%20%240.1%24%20m%20from%20equilibrium%20and%20released%20from%20rest.%20Write%20the%20IVP%2C%20simulate%20the%20motion%20with%20%24c%3D0%24%2C%20and%20then%20find%20a%20damping%20value%20that%20removes%20visible%20oscillation.%0A%0A%20%20%20%208.%20**Compare%20solvers%20on%20an%20oscillator.**%20Compare%20semi-implicit%20Euler%20and%20%60solve_ivp%60%20on%20the%20same%20mass-spring-damper%20system.%20Which%20method%20changes%20more%20when%20you%20increase%20the%20step%20size%3F%20Which%20result%20would%20you%20use%20as%20a%20reference%20solution%3F%0A%0A%20%20%20%209.%20**Two-mass%20spring-damper%20system.**%20Two%20masses%20move%20on%20a%20horizontal%20line%20and%20are%20connected%20by%20a%20spring%20and%20damper.%20Define%20a%20state%20vector%2C%20write%20the%20first-order%20ODEs%2C%20and%20predict%20what%20happens%20to%20the%20distance%20between%20the%20masses%20when%20damping%20is%20increased.%0A%0A%20%20%20%2010.%20**Simple%20muscle-tendon%20model.**%20Treat%20the%20tendon%20as%20one%20spring%2C%20the%20muscle%20fibers%20as%20another%20spring%2C%20the%20viscous%20tissue%20as%20a%20damper%2C%20and%20the%20contractile%20element%20as%20an%20active%20force.%20Define%20a%20one-dimensional%20IVP%20for%20tendon%20length%20and%20explain%20what%20each%20parameter%20represents.%0A%0A%20%20%20%2011.%20**Force-platform%20record.**%20A%20force%20platform%20measures%20vertical%20ground%20reaction%20force%20during%20a%20jump.%20Given%20body%20mass%20and%20the%20force-time%20curve%2C%20write%20the%20ODE%20for%20the%20center-of-mass%20acceleration.%20What%20numerical%20integrations%20would%20you%20perform%20to%20estimate%20takeoff%20velocity%20and%20jump%20height%3F%0A%0A%20%20%20%2012.%20**Your%20own%20movement%20model.**%20Create%20your%20own%20IVP%20from%20a%20movement%20you%20care%20about.%20Define%20the%20state%20variables%2C%20initial%20conditions%2C%20model%20parameters%2C%20and%20one%20parameter%20you%20would%20like%20to%20estimate%20from%20data.%0A%20%20%20%20%22%22%22)%0A%20%20%20%20return%0A%0A%0A%40app.cell(hide_code%3DTrue)%0Adef%20_(mo)%3A%0A%20%20%20%20mo.md(r%22%22%22%0A%20%20%20%20%2F%2F%2F%20details%20%7C%20Final%20answers%20to%20Problems%0A%20%20%20%201.%20An%20ODE%20supplies%20the%20rate%20law%20and%20initial%20conditions%20select%20a%20trajectory.%20A%20pendulum%20released%20from%20different%20initial%20angles%20has%20different%20amplitude%20and%20energy.%0A%20%20%20%202.%20Initial%20angular%20velocity%20changes%20energy%2C%20phase%2C%20and%20possibly%20whether%20full%20rotations%20occur.%20At%2010%C2%B0%20the%20motion%20is%20approximately%20sinusoidal%3B%2045%C2%B0%20and%2090%C2%B0%20increasingly%20depart%20from%20the%20small-angle%20approximation%20and%20have%20longer%20periods.%0A%20%20%20%203.%20Heights%20above%20launch%20level%2C%20using%20%24g%3D9.8%24%20m%2Fs%C2%B2%3A%20127.55%20m%20without%20drag%3B%20113.61%20m%20with%20the%20stated%20quadratic%20drag.%20Downward%20terminal%20velocity%20is%20approximately%20%E2%88%9298.995%20m%2Fs%3B%20reaching%20it%20requires%20sufficient%20falling%20distance.%0A%20%20%20%204.%20Example%20criterion%3A%20at%20matched%20grid%20times%20through%204%20s%2C%20position%20error%20below%200.02%20m.%20For%20the%20constant-gravity%20forward%20Euler%20example%2C%20%24h%3D0.001%24%20s%20meets%20that%20criterion.%20A%20different%20accuracy%20requirement%20gives%20a%20different%20acceptable%20step.%0A%20%20%20%205.%20For%20vector%20quadratic%20drag%20with%20%24k%3D%5Crho%20C_dA%2F2%24%2C%20state%20%24(x%2Cy%2Cv_x%2Cv_y)%24%20has%20derivative%20%24(v_x%2Cv_y%2C-k%5C%7Cv%5C%7Cv_x%2Fm%2C-g-k%5C%7Cv%5C%7Cv_y%2Fm)%24.%20Specify%20four%20initial%20values.%0A%20%20%20%206.%20One%20valid%20choice%20is%20%24k%3D50%24%20N%2Fm%20and%20%24c%3D20%24%20Ns%2Fm%20for%20%24m%3D2%24%20kg%3A%20critical%20damping%20and%20no%20free%20oscillation.%20%E2%80%9CClose%E2%80%9D%20still%20needs%20a%20displacement%20tolerance%20and%20observation%20time.%0A%20%20%20%207.%20%24%5Cdot%20x%3Dv%24%2C%20%24%5Cdot%20v%3D-100x-cv%24%2C%20%24x(0)%3D0.1%24%20m%2C%20%24v(0)%3D0%24.%20With%20%24c%3D0%24%2C%20%24x%3D0.1%5Ccos(10t)%24%20m.%20Critical%20damping%20is%20%24c%3D20%24%20Ns%2Fm.%0A%20%20%20%208.%20Semi-implicit%20Euler%20changes%20more%20with%20its%20integration%20step.%20A%20%60solve_ivp%60%20result%20with%20tightened%20tolerances%20and%20demonstrated%20convergence%20is%20a%20useful%20reference%3B%20output%20spacing%20alone%20is%20not%20its%20internal%20integration%20step.%0A%20%20%20%209.%20Let%20%24q%3Dx_2-x_1-L_0%24%20and%20%24f%3Dkq%2Bc(v_2-v_1)%24.%20Then%20%24(%5Cdot%20x_1%2C%5Cdot%20x_2%2C%5Cdot%20v_1%2C%5Cdot%20v_2)%3D(v_1%2Cv_2%2Cf%2Fm_1%2C-f%2Fm_2)%24.%20Increasing%20damping%20suppresses%20relative%20oscillation%2C%20while%20excessive%20damping%20slows%20relaxation.%0A%20%20%20%2010.%20One%20massless%20series%20example%20uses%20tendon%20extension%20%24x%24%20and%20fixed%20total%20extension%20%24L%24%3A%20%24%5Cdot%20x%3D%5Bk_m(L-x)%2BF_a(t)-k_t%20x%5D%2Fc%24%2C%20%24x(0)%3Dx_0%24.%20Here%20%24k_t%2Ck_m%24%20are%20stiffnesses%2C%20%24c%24%20is%20muscle-side%20viscosity%2C%20and%20%24F_a%24%20is%20active%20force.%20This%20is%20one%20stated%20model%2C%20not%20a%20unique%20consequence%20of%20the%20verbal%20description.%0A%20%20%20%2011.%20%24%5Cdot%20v%3DF_z%2Fm-g%24%20and%20%24%5Cdot%20y%3Dv%24.%20Integrate%20from%20known%20initial%20velocity%20and%20position%3B%20after%20takeoff%2C%20ballistic%20rise%20is%20%24v_%7Bto%7D%5E2%2F(2g)%24%20when%20drag%20is%20neglected.%0A%20%20%20%2012.%20Example%3A%20damped%20knee-angle%20relaxation%20with%20state%20%24(%5Ctheta%2C%5Comega)%24%2C%20%24%5Cdot%5Ctheta%3D%5Comega%24%2C%20%24I%5Cdot%5Comega%3D-b%5Comega-k%5Ctheta%24%2C%20stated%20initial%20angle%20and%20velocity%2C%20and%20damping%20%24b%24%20estimated%20from%20the%20measured%20decay.%20Other%20well-defined%20IVPs%20are%20valid.%0A%0A%20%20%20%20%2F%2F%2F%0A%20%20%20%20%22%
